chief_complaint: lower back pain post-lifting, negative SLR, no red flags
hpi_details: 42-year-old male construction worker presents to the primary care clinic with acute, localized lower back pain that started 2 days ago immediately after lifting a heavy box using poor form. He denies any radiating pain down his legs, numbness, tingling, or bowel/bladder incontinence.
ideas: He thinks he might have slipped a disc or popped something out of place in his spine when he lifted the crate with poor form.
concerns: He is worried that he will not be able to do heavy lifting and could lose his construction job if his back does not heal quickly.
expectations: He hopes to get an X-ray to make sure nothing is broken and a doctor's note for light duties so he does not miss work.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Lumbar Strain evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Lumbar Strain is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes avoiding early imaging in the absence of red flags (Choosing Wisely), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: lower back pain post-lifting, negative SLR, no red flags

Key HPI features: A 42-year-old male presents to the clinic with lower back pain post-lifting, negative SLR, and no red flags. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Normal vitals, bilateral lumbar paraspinal muscle spasm and tenderness, negative straight leg raise bilaterally, normal lower-extremity strength/sensation/reflexes.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Lumbar Strain.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Disc herniation without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel incontinence, or bilateral leg weakness — suggests cauda equina syndrome and needs emergent imaging and surgical referral.
management_principles: Choosing Wisely: avoid early imaging in the absence of red flags
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 42M presenting with acute, non-radiating lower back pain following a known lifting injury.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Exam reveals bilateral lumbar paraspinal muscle spasm and tenderness. Straight Leg Raise (SLR) test is negative bilaterally. Neurological exam (strength, sensation, reflexes) in the lower extremities is entirely normal.
reference_soap.plan: Reassurance that mechanical back pain is benign and self-limiting. Avoid bed rest; advise returning to normal activities as tolerated. Prescribe oral NSAIDs (Naproxen) on a scheduled basis. Recommend superficial heat application and back strengthening exercises.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Acute Lumbar Strain FM
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Acute Lumbar Strain FM

teaching.one_liner: Mechanical back pain after lifting, without red flags, managed with reassurance and staying active rather than imaging.
red_flags: Saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel incontinence, or bilateral leg weakness — suggests cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency
Fever, IV drug use, or recent spinal procedure — raises concern for spinal epidural abscess
History of cancer or unexplained weight loss — raises concern for spinal metastasis
Age over 50 with significant trauma or osteoporosis — raises concern for vertebral compression fracture

must_ask.say: Did this start after lifting something?
Does it go down your leg?
Any changes in bladder or bowel control?
What worries you about this pain?

history.answer: I hurt my lower back two days ago while lifting a heavy box at work, and it has been aching constantly ever since.
The pain is across my lower back on both sides of my spine, and it stays right there without traveling down into my buttocks or legs.
It started suddenly two days ago when I bent over with poor form to hoist a heavy box at my construction job.
It feels like a deep, tight ache with sharp spasms when I try to twist or move around. I would rate it about a 6 out of 10.
Bending forward, standing for long periods, or lifting anything makes it worse. Lying flat on a firm bed or resting with a heating pad brings slight relief.
It does not wake me up from a sound sleep at night, although finding a comfortable sleeping position can be difficult.
My back feels stiff for about ten or fifteen minutes when I first get out of bed, but it loosens up once I move around.
No, I have not had any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my legs or feet.
No, I have normal feeling around my groin and private area, and my bowel and bladder control is completely normal.
My back feels tight when walking, but my legs do not get tired or numb, and bending forward does not relieve any leg symptoms.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss.
No, I have never had cancer or any history of tumors.
No, I have not had any recent infections, spinal procedures, or epidural shots, and I have never used intravenous or illicit drugs.
No, I do not have osteoporosis, I have never taken steroid pills, and I did not suffer a fall or direct blow to my back.
No, I do not have any belly pain, no pulsating sensation in my stomach, and no burning or blood in my urine.
No red or painful eyes, no heel or joint pain, no long-standing diarrhea, and no skin rashes like psoriasis.
I took some over-the-counter ibuprofen yesterday, and it helped take the edge off the pain for a few hours.
I work in commercial construction doing heavy manual labor, which involves constant lifting and bending.
I am stressed about missing work and letting down my crew, but otherwise my mood is stable.
I felt something give way when I lifted that heavy box awkwardly, so I thought I might have slipped a disc in my lower back.
I'm really worried that if I can't do the heavy lifting at work, my foreman will let me go and I won't be able to provide for my family.
I'm hoping to get an X-ray to check my spine and a doctor's note for light duty so I can stay on the job site without having to lift heavy loads.
I have never been diagnosed with any chronic health conditions, high blood pressure, or diabetes.
I have never had any operations, and I have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any regular prescription medications or herbal supplements, just the ibuprofen I tried yesterday.
I have no known allergies to medications.
No, I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink alcohol socially, usually two or three beers on the weekend with friends.
I live in an apartment with my wife and our two young children.
My parents are both in good health in their seventies, with no family history of chronic spine disorders or autoimmune conditions.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.7 °C, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air.
Normal spinal alignment with bilateral lumbar paraspinal muscle spasm and tenderness; no midline vertebral spinous process tenderness, and straight leg raise test is negative bilaterally.
Active lumbar flexion and extension are restricted secondary to lower back pain, while lateral bending is mildly limited.
Lower extremity motor strength is 5/5 bilaterally across all tested muscle groups, including hip flexors, quadriceps, and ankle dorsiflexors and plantarflexors.
Intact sensation to light touch and pinprick across bilateral L1 through S1 dermatomes, with normal perineal sensation.
Patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally, with down-going plantar reflexes.
Soft, non-tender abdomen without palpable mass, guarding, or pulsatile abdominal aortic enlargement.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion bilaterally.
